title: Article Allotment
intro: A, an, the, or nothing at all. Pick the article each sentence really needs.

A2.q: I have ___ dog and two cats.
A2.why: First mention of one of many dogs: “a”, and “dog” starts with a consonant sound.
“Apple” starts with a vowel sound, so “an”; a single countable noun can't go without an article.
There is only one sun, so it takes “the”.
Jobs take “a/an” in English: “Es médico” becomes “He's a doctor”.

A2.q: I saw ___ elephant at the zoo.

A2.why: We both know which door, the one in this room: “the”.
One flat among many: “a”, never “live in small flat”. “Small” starts with a consonant sound.
Jobs need an article, and “engineer” starts with a vowel sound: “an”.

A2.q: Where is ___ bathroom in your flat?
A2.why: The flat has one bathroom we both know about: “the”.

A2.q: My great-grandfather was ___ cowboy in Texas.
A2.why: A job, so “a”: never “was cowboy” as in Spanish “era vaquero”.

A2.q: I eat ___ orange from Valencia every morning.
A2.why: “Orange” starts with a vowel sound, so “an”.

B1.why: Music in general takes no article.

B1.q: In general, ___ dogs are loyal animals.
B1.why: “In general” is the clue: plural nouns used generally take no article.

B1.q: My grandson is eight, and he goes to ___ school by bus.
B1.why: A pupil goes to school for its normal purpose: no article.

B1.q: We need ___ information about flights to London.
I bought ___ new car last week.
B1.why: First mention of one car: “a”, and “new” starts with a consonant sound.

B1.q: ___ book on the table is mine.
B1.why: “On the table” tells us exactly which book: “the”.

B1.q: She's afraid of ___ spiders, big or small.
B1.why: Spiders in general, “big or small”: plural with no article.
Any umbrella will do, and “umbrella” starts with a vowel sound: “an”.

B1.q: In the Wild West, ___ life was hard for farmers.
B1.why: “Life” in general takes no article, unlike Spanish “la vida”.
Sports and games take no article: “play tennis”.

B2.q: He went to ___ prison for three years.
B2.why: He was a prisoner, so prison is used for its purpose: no article.

B2.q: His wife went to ___ prison every week to visit him.
B2.why: She only visits the building, so “the”; “went to prison” would mean she was locked up.

B2.q: ___ more you practise, the better you get.
B2.why: Comparative pairs use “the ... the”: “the more you practise, the better you get”.

B2.q: She was appointed ___ head of the department last year.
B2.why: A unique role after “appoint” or “elect” takes no article: “appointed head of the department”.
Life in general, an abstract idea: no article.
After “play”, British English normally uses “the” with instruments: “play the guitar”.

B2.q: It was such ___ lovely evening that we ate outside.
B2.why: “Such” + a singular countable noun needs “a”: “such a lovely evening”.
“Weather” is uncountable, so the exclamation takes no article: “What awful weather!”
History is general, but “of Spain” makes it specific: “the”.

B2.q: She hopes to become ___ MP one day.
B2.why: “MP” is said “em-pee”, a vowel sound, so “an”.

B2.q: We had ___ lovely lunch at a little restaurant in El Palmar.
B2.why: Meals normally take no article, but with an adjective they take “a”: “a lovely lunch”.

C1.why: Patience in general, an abstract idea: no article.

C1.q: He has ___ patience of a saint.
C1.why: “Of a saint” makes it a specific kind of patience: “the”.
Unemployment as a general phenomenon takes no article.
Fixed phrase “have an eye for”, and “eye” starts with a vowel sound.
“By candlelight” is a fixed phrase with no article.
“The” + adjective means the whole group of people: the rich, the poor.

C1.q: He was taken to ___ hospital after the accident and kept in for a week.
C1.why: British English usually says “to hospital” for a patient, with no article.

C1.q: I went to ___ hospital to visit him.
C1.why: A visitor goes to the building, so “the”; “went to hospital” would make you the patient.

C1.q: On ___ whole, the trip was a success.
C1.why: Fixed phrase “on the whole”, meaning generally.

C1.q: She made ___ point of thanking everyone.
C1.why: Fixed phrase “make a point of” doing something.

C1.q: In ___ Middle Ages, doctors believed disease came from bad air.
C1.why: Named historical periods take “the”: the Middle Ages.

C1.q: The sheriff was ___ man of few words.
C1.why: Fixed phrase “a man of few words”: one quiet man among many.
